subChunks.title: Defining & Classifying Psychological Disorders
subChunks.hookHtml: In 1851, Samuel Cartwright, a Louisiana physician, published an article in the New Orleans Medical and Surgical Journal describing a mental disorder he called 'drapetomania' — a psychiatric condition afflicting enslaved Black people, characterised by an irrational urge to flee from their enslavers. His recommended treatment included whipping. In 1952, the first Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-I) listed homosexuality as a sociopathic personality disturbance. It remained in the DSM until 1973, when the American Psychiatric Association voted to remove it — following sustained advocacy from LGBTQ+ activists and the embarrassing finding that mental health professionals could not reliably distinguish gay from straight people in blind interviews. These historical examples are not aberrations — they illustrate that the boundaries of 'mental disorder' have always been contested, politically shaped, and subject to cultural assumptions. Understanding how psychologists and psychiatrists define, classify, and diagnose psychological disorders — and the limits of these processes — is foundational knowledge.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Defining Abnormality: The Four Ds

There is no universally agreed definition of psychological disorder. Common criteria include:

Distress       — The person is significantly suffering. But some disorders involve
                 little subjective distress (e.g., psychopathy); some normal states
                 involve great distress (grief).

Dysfunction    — Behaviour interferes with daily functioning. But dysfunction
                 depends on context — 'extreme' commitment to a cause might be
                 dysfunctional by conventional metrics.

Deviance       — Behaviour is statistically uncommon or violates social norms.
                 But deviance is culturally relative, and rarity alone is not
                 pathological (genius is statistically rare).

Danger         — Risk of harm to self or others. But most people with mental
                 disorders are not dangerous; this criterion vastly overestimates
                 the link between disorder and violence.

The most defensible position is that psychological disorder requires multiple criteria simultaneously, none of which is sufficient alone. The DSM-5 (2013) defines a mental disorder as a clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion regulation, or behaviour that reflects a dysfunction in psychological, biological, or developmental processes and is associated with significant distress or disability — while explicitly excluding culturally expected responses to common stressors.

Classification Systems: DSM and ICD

Two major classification systems organise psychological disorders:

DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition, APA, 2013): The dominant system in the USA and much of the English-speaking world. Provides operationalised diagnostic criteria (symptom checklists with thresholds) for over 300 disorders, organised into diagnostic categories.

ICD-11 (International Classification of Diseases, 11th edition, WHO, 2019): The international standard; covers all health conditions, with a dedicated mental and behavioural disorders chapter. More widely used globally, particularly in Europe and low-to-middle-income countries.

Both systems use categorical diagnosis — you either meet criteria for a disorder or you don't. Critics argue this misrepresents the dimensional nature of psychological symptoms (distress lies on a continuum, not a binary), leads to diagnostic boundary disputes (e.g., what distinguishes ADHD from normative childhood hyperactivity?), and encourages over-diagnosis through diagnostic creep (lowering thresholds over successive editions).

Major Diagnostic Categories (DSM-5)

Depressive disorders         — Major Depressive Disorder, PDD, PMDD
Anxiety disorders            — GAD, Panic Disorder, Phobias, Social Anxiety
OCD and related              — OCD, BDD, Hoarding
Trauma-related               — PTSD, Acute Stress Disorder, Adjustment Disorders
Psychotic disorders          — Schizophrenia Spectrum
Bipolar and related          — Bipolar I, II, Cyclothymia
Neurodevelopmental           — ADHD, ASD, Intellectual Disability
Personality disorders        — Antisocial, Borderline, Narcissistic
Substance-related            — Substance Use Disorders, Addictions
Dissociative disorders       — DID, Depersonalisation
Eating disorders             — Anorexia, Bulimia, BED

Reliability and Validity of Psychiatric Diagnosis

Reliability refers to the consistency of diagnosis — do two clinicians applying the same criteria reach the same conclusion? Earlier DSM editions had poor inter-rater reliability. DSM-III (1980) introduced operational criteria partly to address this. DSM-5 field trials showed mixed reliability, with kappas (agreement coefficients) ranging from excellent for PTSD (κ = 0.67) to poor for some personality disorders (κ = 0.28–0.40).

Validity refers to whether diagnostic categories capture meaningfully distinct conditions. Rosenhan's (1973) 'On Being Sane in Insane Places' study — in which pseudopatients feigned hallucinations to gain psychiatric admission, then behaved normally but remained hospitalised — challenged validity dramatically. Critics of the study argue that its methodology was deceptive and that standards have improved substantially. However, concerns about validity persist: comorbidity (the co-occurrence of multiple diagnoses) is the norm rather than the exception, suggesting diagnostic boundaries may not map onto distinct biological conditions.

The Medical Model vs. Biopsychosocial Model

The medical model treats psychological disorders as diseases with biological causes, best treated by biological interventions (medications). It has driven productive research and reduced stigma by framing disorder as illness rather than moral failure. However, it risks reducing complex psychosocial phenomena to neurochemistry, pathologising ordinary human suffering, and ignoring social determinants of mental health (poverty, discrimination, trauma).

The biopsychosocial model (Engel, 1977) proposes that psychological disorder results from the interaction of biological predispositions, psychological factors (cognition, personality, learning history), and social/cultural context. This is the most scientifically defensible and clinically comprehensive framework, though it is harder to operationalise than the medical model.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen reads out, verbatim, a passage from an 1851 medical journal. The room is silent. 'That was published in a peer-reviewed medical journal,' she says. 'And it was accepted.'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: I don't tell you about drapetomania to make you comfortable about the DSM-5. I tell you about it because every diagnostic system reflects the values, power structures, and cultural assumptions of the people who create it. The DSM is better than it was. It is still a human document, produced by a committee, shaped by pharmaceutical industry relationships, advocacy group lobbying, and theoretical debates that are never purely scientific.

storyBeats.speaker: The Rosenhan study
storyBeats.text: David Rosenhan recruited 8 pseudopatients who presented to psychiatric hospitals complaining of hearing a voice say 'thud', 'empty', and 'hollow'. All were admitted, seven diagnosed with schizophrenia. Despite behaving normally from admission onward, they remained hospitalised for an average of 19 days. None were identified as pseudopatients by staff, though several fellow patients suspected them. In a follow-up, hospitals told of the study challenged Rosenhan to send pseudopatients — none were sent, yet the hospitals identified 41 'suspected pseudopatients' out of 193 new patients. The study exposed the stickiness of psychiatric labels and the power of context to shape clinical judgement.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The biopsychosocial model is harder to use in a busy clinic than the medical model. But it's more true. Depression is not just low serotonin. It's low serotonin interacting with a history of childhood adversity, interacting with a work environment with no autonomy, interacting with a culture that stigmatises help-seeking. You can't medicate social determinants.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A clinical psychologist is assessing a 32-year-old woman, Sara, who has not left her flat for three weeks, is not eating regularly, is crying frequently, and has stopped responding to calls from friends. She reports that this began after she was made redundant at work.

  1. Using the Four Ds framework, assess whether Sara's presentation meets criteria for psychological disorder. Identify which criteria are clearly met and which are ambiguous.
  2. A psychiatrist proposes diagnosing Sara with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). What questions about reliability and validity should the psychologist keep in mind when considering this diagnosis?
  3. How would the medical model and the biopsychosocial model each explain Sara's difficulties, and what treatment implications would each model have?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Distress is clearly met — Sara is crying frequently and has withdrawn socially, indicating significant subjective suffering. Dysfunction is clearly met — she has stopped eating regularly, is not leaving her flat, and has withdrawn from friends; these represent significant impairments in self-care, social functioning, and daily activities. Deviance/statistical rarity is ambiguous — social withdrawal and tearfulness after job loss are common and may represent a normative grief-like response to a significant stressor rather than pathological behaviour. Danger is not apparent — there is no indication of risk to self or others, though given the severity of withdrawal, self-neglect (not eating) merits monitoring. The key clinical question is whether Sara's presentation exceeds what would be considered a culturally expected and proportionate response to redundancy — which the DSM-5 requires ruling out before diagnosing MDD.

2. On reliability: the psychologist should consider whether two clinicians applying DSM-5 criteria to Sara's presentation would reach the same conclusion. Reliability for MDD is moderate (κ ≈ 0.28 in some DSM-5 field trials). The ambiguity about whether her symptoms represent normal grief (bereavement exclusion was removed from DSM-5) vs. MDD means clinicians may disagree. On validity: MDD is a broad category encompassing considerable heterogeneity — individuals with very different symptom profiles, biological markers, and treatment responses may both receive the same diagnosis. Sara's presentation may or may not share the same underlying mechanism as other MDD diagnoses, limiting the clinical utility of the categorical label.

3. The medical model would explain Sara's difficulties primarily through neurobiological dysfunction — dysregulation of serotonergic, noradrenergic, or dopaminergic systems — and would likely recommend antidepressant medication (e.g., an SSRI) as the primary treatment, possibly alongside brief psychological intervention. The biopsychosocial model would seek to understand Sara's presentation across multiple levels: biological predisposition (e.g., genetic vulnerability to depression, sleep disruption affecting neurochemistry); psychological factors (negative cognitive appraisals of the redundancy — 'I'm worthless', 'I'll never find work again'); and social factors (social isolation, financial insecurity, potential absence of social support). Treatment would be multi-modal: addressing biological factors (sleep, nutrition, medication if warranted), cognitive factors (CBT to address distorted appraisals), and social factors (reconnecting with support network, practical help with job searching). The biopsychosocial approach is more comprehensive but also more demanding of clinician time and patient engagement.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The process of adding new diagnoses to the DSM has been criticised as 'medicalising normal human experience'. Evaluate this critique with reference to at least two specific examples (e.g., ADHD, PTSD, grief disorder, internet gaming disorder). In your answer, consider both the benefits of diagnosis and the concerns about over-pathologising. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The critique that the DSM medicalises normal human experience has genuine force, though the picture is more nuanced than critics sometimes acknowledge.

Some examples support the critique. The removal of the bereavement exclusion from DSM-5 MDD criteria means clinically significant grief responses after bereavement can now be diagnosed as Major Depressive Disorder after just two weeks — a threshold that many argue pathologises a universal human experience. Internet Gaming Disorder was included in DSM-5 as a condition requiring further study — critics note that the underlying research base is thin and that reframing heavy game use as 'disorder' medicalises what may be a coping behaviour or social phenomenon. The dramatic increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades, particularly in the USA, has raised concerns about diagnostic thresholds, pharmaceutical industry influence, and cultural expectations of children's behaviour.

However, the case for diagnosis should not be dismissed. ADHD, when rigorously assessed, identifies a genuinely disabling condition that responds to evidence-based treatment; without diagnosis, many individuals — particularly girls, who present differently — suffer unnecessarily and receive no support. PTSD recognition transformed the treatment of war veterans and survivors of assault who were previously told their suffering was a character weakness. Diagnosis can reduce stigma (framing suffering as illness rather than failure) and provide access to treatment and legal protections.

The key tension is between the benefits of identification and the harms of false positives, over-medication, and the social normalisation of psychiatric labels. The solution is likely not less diagnosis but more rigorous and contextually sensitive application of diagnostic criteria, combined with dimensional approaches that capture the full range of severity.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what it means for a behaviour or feeling to be classified as a 'mental disorder'. Use at least two of the Four Ds (distress, dysfunction, deviance, danger) to explain why this is a more complicated question than it might first appear.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The co-occurrence of two or more diagnosable conditions in the same individual. Extremely common in clinical populations — the norm rather than the exception. Challenges categorical diagnostic models.

Sociological perspective (Szasz, Scheff) that psychiatric diagnosis is a social label with profound consequences for identity and treatment: once labelled, behaviour is interpreted through the diagnostic lens, potentially creating self-fulfilling effects.

The degree of agreement between two or more independent clinicians applying the same diagnostic criteria to the same patient. Expressed as Cohen's kappa (κ); κ > 0.6 is considered acceptable for clinical purposes.

The debate about whether psychological disorders are best conceived as discrete categories (you have it or you don't) or as dimensions (everyone falls somewhere on a continuum). The HiTOP model and RDoC framework represent dimensional alternatives to DSM categorical diagnosis.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is the most widely used classification system for mental disorders in the United States?
questions.explanationHtml: The DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition), published by the American Psychiatric Association, is the dominant classification system in the United States and much of the English-speaking world. The ICD-11 (WHO) is the international standard used more widely globally. PDM-2 is a psychodynamically-oriented alternative used by some clinicians. RDoC is a research framework developed by NIMH to organise mental disorder research around biological and psychological dimensions rather than categorical diagnoses.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A behaviour that is statistically rare or culturally deviant is, by itself, sufficient grounds for a diagnosis of psychological disorder.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Statistical rarity or cultural deviance alone is not sufficient for a psychological disorder diagnosis. Genius, creativity, and moral courage are statistically rare but not disordered. Culturally non-conforming behaviour may be culturally deviant without causing distress or dysfunction. The DSM-5 requires that the behaviour reflect a dysfunction in psychological, biological, or developmental processes AND be associated with significant distress or disability. Deviance is one criterion among several, none of which is sufficient alone.

questions.questionHtml: Rosenhan's (1973) pseudopatient study is often cited as evidence against the validity of psychiatric diagnosis. Which of the following is the strongest methodological critique of using the Rosenhan study for this purpose?
options: The pseudopatients were not trained clinicians
Presenting with fabricated hallucinations is deceptive — genuine diagnostic validity cannot be assessed from data obtained through deception
Psychiatrists would not make these errors today because diagnostic criteria have improved significantly
The sample was too small to draw conclusions about psychiatric diagnosis generally
questions.correctAnswer: Psychiatrists would not make these errors today because diagnostic criteria have improved significantly
questions.explanationHtml: The strongest critique is that Rosenhan's study was conducted in 1973, before the operationalised diagnostic criteria introduced in DSM-III (1980) and further refined in DSM-IV and DSM-5. Modern diagnostic interviews are more structured and reliability has improved substantially. The deception critique (option B) is ethically valid but doesn't undermine the study's findings about the system as it then was — deception was the only way to investigate clinicians' judgements naturalistically. The sample size critique (option D) is secondary. Option A is irrelevant — the pseudopatients weren't pretending to be clinicians. The temporal limitation (option C) is the strongest evidence-based counter-argument to using this 1973 study as a definitive indictment of contemporary psychiatric diagnosis.
